modules.title: Applying: The Letter That Goes With the CV
modules.description: A CV that clears the ATS gets you into the pile. What happens next is an application and an interview, and this course stopped before either. This module covers the letter, and how to walk into the room already prepared.

lessons.title: Writing a Cover Letter Somebody Reads
lessons.description: Format, structure and what actually belongs in a cover letter — from Indeed, the job board itself. Includes when a cover letter helps and when it is wasted effort.
objectives: Structure a cover letter in three parts: why this job, why you, what happens next
Tailor a letter to one advertised role instead of sending one generic letter everywhere
Judge when a cover letter is worth writing and when the application form makes it redundant
lessons.notes:
The rule that saves the most time: one letter per role, and the tailoring is mostly in the first paragraph. Name the specific job, name the specific reason you want THIS employer, and then evidence one claim from the advert with something you have actually done. A letter that could be sent to any employer will be read as exactly that.

What not to do, and it is the most common mistake: do not restate the CV in prose. The reader already has the CV. The letter's job is the part the CV cannot carry — why you are applying here, and any explanation the CV raises (a gap, a change of field, a move).

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — applying from Kenya, where much of the market is not a formal ATS. A great many jobs here are advertised on LinkedIn, on company websites, in Facebook groups and by WhatsApp forward, and the "cover letter" is the body of an email or a short message. The structure still applies, compressed: which role, why you, one piece of evidence, and a clear closing line. Keep the CV as a PDF attachment named with your own name — Achieng_Otieno_CV.pdf, not Document1.pdf — because the file name is the first thing the recruiter sees in a crowded inbox.

Where a form asks for a "cover note" in a text box, write it in the same structure, but shorter. Nobody reads six paragraphs in a text box.
lessons.practice: Find one real job advert you could plausibly apply for — LinkedIn, BrighterMonday, or a company careers page. Write a cover letter of no more than 250 words in three parts: why this role at this employer, one specific piece of evidence that you can do it, and a closing line saying what you would like to happen next. Then delete every sentence that merely repeats something already on your CV, and see how much is left. If more than half went, the letter was doing the CV's job instead of its own.

quiz.question: What is the cover letter's job that the CV cannot do?
options: Listing your qualifications in date order
Explaining why you are applying to this specific employer, and addressing anything the CV raises
Repeating your work history in full sentences
Providing your contact details

quiz.question: You are applying by email rather than through a formal system. What should the covering message do?
options: Be omitted entirely, since the CV is attached
Be as long as a formal letter, to show effort
Follow the same structure, compressed — which role, why you, one piece of evidence, a clear closing line
Contain only the job title

lessons.title: Preparing Before the Interview, Not During It
lessons.description: Indeed's pre-interview strategy: the research, the questions to have ready, and the practical preparation that decides how the first five minutes go.
objectives: Research an employer well enough to ask one specific, informed question
Prepare evidence for the requirements named in the job advert
Prepare the practical logistics so nothing avoidable goes wrong on the day
lessons.notes:
Preparation is mostly one exercise: take the job advert, list every requirement it names, and write one thing you have actually done against each. That list is where almost every answer in the interview will come from. If a requirement has nothing against it, decide now how you will answer honestly — what you have done that is closest, and how you would get up to speed.

Have two or three questions ready to ask them. "What does a good first three months look like in this role?" is worth more than anything from a list of clever questions online, because the answer tells you what you would actually be judged on.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — preparing for an interview that happens over a patchy connection. Most remote interviews for Kenyan candidates happen on Zoom, Google Meet or WhatsApp video, and the connection is a real risk. Test the app on the actual device the day before, not an hour before. Sit where the light is in front of you, not behind. Have your phone charged and enough data or a bundle loaded. Send the interviewer your phone number in advance and say plainly that if the video drops you will call — that one line turns a technical failure from a disaster into a small inconvenience, and it reads as competence rather than an excuse.

For a face-to-face interview, do the journey in your head with real Nairobi traffic and then add an hour. Arriving early and waiting is free; arriving late is not recoverable.
lessons.practice: Take one real job advert. Write out every requirement it lists, one per line. Against each, write one specific thing you have done — a task, a project, a result, with a number if you have one. Mark any requirement you cannot answer, and write two sentences for it: what is closest in your experience, and how you would close the gap. Finally, write three questions you would ask them. Keep this page; the next module turns these into answers.

quiz.question: What is the most useful single preparation exercise before an interview?
options: Memorising the company's history
Rehearsing a script for every possible question
Listing each requirement from the advert and writing one thing you have actually done against it
Preparing a list of salary figures

quiz.question: Why tell an interviewer in advance that you will call if the video connection drops?
options: It is a legal requirement for remote interviews
It turns a likely technical failure into a small inconvenience, and reads as preparedness rather than an excuse
It lets you avoid the video interview altogether
It guarantees a better connection

modules.title: Answering the Questions
modules.description: The questions almost every interview asks, and the one technique that turns a vague answer into evidence. Both from Indeed's own channel.

lessons.title: The Questions Almost Every Interview Asks
lessons.description: Six questions that come up in nearly every interview, what the interviewer is actually trying to find out with each, and how to answer without waffle.
objectives: Recognise what an interviewer is really asking behind each common question
Answer "tell me about yourself" in under two minutes, aimed at the role
Give an honest answer to the weakness question without either boasting or self-harm
lessons.notes:
Every common question has a real question behind it. "Tell me about yourself" is not an invitation to your life story — it means "why are you in this room". Keep it to a short arc: what you do, one piece of evidence, why this role. Under two minutes.

"What is your greatest weakness" is asking whether you can see yourself accurately and do something about it. The failed answers are the boast disguised as a flaw ("I work too hard") and the genuine disqualifier ("I miss deadlines"). The working answer is a real, non-fatal weakness plus the specific thing you now do about it.

"Why do you want to work here" is checking you have done any research at all. One specific fact about the employer beats three sentences of enthusiasm.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — the salary question, which is asked earlier and more bluntly in Kenya than in the markets these videos are made for. You will often be asked your expectation in a first call. Have a researched range ready rather than a single figure, say it calmly, and add that you are open to discussing it against the full package. Do not answer with "whatever you offer" — it reads as having no idea what the work is worth, and it is the answer most likely to get you underpaid. If you genuinely do not know the range, ask what they have budgeted for the role; that is a fair and normal question.
lessons.practice: Record yourself on your phone answering three questions: tell me about yourself, why do you want this job, and what is your greatest weakness. Then listen back with a timer. Cut "tell me about yourself" to under two minutes. For the weakness answer, check that you named something real AND said what you do about it. Recording yourself is uncomfortable and it is the fastest way to hear the waffle you cannot hear while speaking.

quiz.question: What is "tell me about yourself" actually asking?
options: For your full life story in chronological order
For your hobbies and personal interests
Why you are in this room — a short arc of what you do, one piece of evidence, and why this role
For a summary of your salary history

quiz.question: You are asked your salary expectation in a first call. What is the strongest response?
options: "Whatever you think is fair"
A researched range, said calmly, with openness to discussing the full package
The highest figure you can think of
Refusing to discuss money until an offer is made

lessons.title: STAR: Turning a Claim Into Evidence
lessons.description: The technique behind behavioural interview questions — "tell me about a time when…" — and how to structure an answer so it lands as evidence rather than a claim.
objectives: Structure an answer as Situation, Task, Action, Result
Choose the right example for the requirement being tested
State a result concretely, with a number where one exists
lessons.notes:
STAR is the highest-value single technique in this whole course, and it is what most candidates who fail interviews are missing. Situation: where and when, in one sentence. Task: what you specifically had to do. Action: what YOU did — not the team, you. Result: what changed, with a number if one exists.

The two failure modes are worth naming. Answers that stop at Action leave the interviewer to guess whether it worked. Answers that say "we" throughout leave them unable to tell what you personally contributed. Say "I" for your own actions even when the work was collaborative; that is accuracy, not arrogance.

A result does not have to be a triumph. "We missed the deadline by two days instead of two weeks" is a result. "It did not work, and here is what I changed afterwards" is a result, and a strong answer to a question about failure.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO — where to get examples when you have never held a formal job. This is the position most learners on this platform are in, and it is not a barrier. STAR examples can come from a family business, a church or mosque committee, a school project, a chama, a side hustle, volunteering, or work you did on this platform. The interviewer is testing whether you can handle a situation, not whether you were paid at the time. Say where it happened plainly and use the same structure.

Build a bank of six examples covering: solving a problem, handling a difficult person, missing a target, learning something quickly, taking initiative, and working under pressure. Six will cover almost any behavioural question you are asked.
lessons.practice: Using the requirement list you built in the previous module, write out six STAR answers — one per line of the structure, so you can see whether each part is really there. At least one must be about something that did not go well. Then check every answer for two things: does it end with a result, and does it say what YOU did rather than what the team did? Rewrite any that fail either test.

quiz.question: What does the R in STAR require?
options: A reference who can confirm the story
What changed as a result, stated concretely and with a number where one exists
The reason you left that job
A repeat of the situation for emphasis

quiz.question: You have never held a formal job. Where can STAR examples come from?
options: Nowhere — behavioural questions cannot be answered without employment
Only from internships and formal work placements
A family business, a committee, a school project, a chama, volunteering or a side hustle — the test is whether you can handle the situation, not whether you were paid
You should invent a plausible workplace example
